13:31.ar: وَلَوۡ أَنَّ قُرۡءَانࣰ ا سُيِّرَتۡ بِهِ ٱلۡجِبَالُ أَوۡ قُطِّعَتۡ بِهِ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ أَوۡ كُلِّمَ بِهِ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰۗ بَل لِّلَّهِ ٱلۡأَمۡرُ جَمِيعًاۗ أَفَلَمۡ يَاْيۡـَٔسِ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ أَن لَّوۡ يَشَآءُ ٱللَّهُ لَهَدَى ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعࣰ اۗ وَلَا يَزَالُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ تُصِيبُهُم بِمَا صَنَعُواْ قَارِعَةٌ أَوۡ تَحُلُّ قَرِيبࣰ ا مِّن دَارِهِمۡ حَتَّىٰ يَأۡتِيَ وَعۡدُ ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُخۡلِفُ ٱلۡمِيعَادَ
13:31.en: Had it been possible for a Lecture to cause the mountains to move, or the earth to be torn asunder, or the dead to speak, (this Qur'an would have done so). Nay, but Allah's is the whole command. Do not those who believe know that, had Allah willed, He could have guided all mankind? As for those who disbelieve, disaster ceaseth not to strike them because of what they do, or it dwelleth near their home until the threat of Allah come to pass. Lo! Allah faileth not to keep the tryst

13:32.ar: وَلَقَدِ ٱسۡتُهۡزِئَ بِرُسُلࣲ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ فَأَمۡلَيۡتُ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ ثُمَّ أَخَذۡتُهُمۡۖ فَكَيۡفَ كَانَ عِقَابِ
13:32.en: And verily messengers (of Allah) were mocked before thee, but long I bore with those who disbelieved. At length I seized them, and how (awful) was My punishment

13:33.ar: أَفَمَنۡ هُوَ قَآئِمٌ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ نَفۡسِۭ بِمَا كَسَبَتۡۗ وَجَعَلُواْ لِلَّهِ شُرَكَآءَ قُلۡ سَمُّوهُمۡۚ أَمۡ تُنَبِّـُٔونَهُۥ بِمَا لَا يَعۡلَمُ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ أَم بِظَٰهِرࣲ مِّنَ ٱلۡقَوۡلِۗ بَلۡ زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ مَكۡرُهُمۡ وَصُدُّواْ عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِۗ وَمَن يُضۡلِلِ ٱللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُۥ مِنۡ هَادࣲ‏
13:33.en: Is He Who is aware of the deserts of every soul (as he who is aware of nothing)? Yet they ascribe unto Allah partners. Say: Name them. Is it that ye would inform Him of something which He knoweth not in the earth? Or is it but a way of speaking? Nay but their contrivance is made seeming fair for those who disbelieve and they are kept from the right road. He whom Allah sendeth astray, for him there is no guide

13:34.ar: لَّهُمۡ عَذَابࣱ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَلَعَذَابُ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ أَشَقُّۖ وَمَا لَهُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ مِن وَاقࣲ‏
13:34.en: For them is torment in the life of the world, and verily the doom of the Hereafter is more painful, and they have no defender from Allah

13:35.ar: ۞مَّثَلُ ٱلۡجَنَّةِ ٱلَّتِي وُعِدَ ٱلۡمُتَّقُونَۖ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِهَا ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُۖ أُكُلُهَا دَآئِمࣱ وَظِلُّهَاۚ تِلۡكَ عُقۡبَى ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَواْۚ وَّعُقۡبَى ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ ٱلنَّارُ
13:35.en: A similitude of the Garden which is promised unto those who keep their duty (to Allah): Underneath it rivers flow; its food is everlasting, and its shade; this is the reward of those who keep their duty, while the reward of disbelievers is the Fire

13:36.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ يَفۡرَحُونَ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيۡكَۖ وَمِنَ ٱلۡأَحۡزَابِ مَن يُنكِرُ بَعۡضَهُۥۚ قُلۡ إِنَّمَآ أُمِرۡتُ أَنۡ أَعۡبُدَ ٱللَّهَ وَلَآ أُشۡرِكَ بِهِۦٓۚ إِلَيۡهِ أَدۡعُواْ وَإِلَيۡهِ مَـَٔابِ
13:36.en: Those unto whom We gave the Scripture rejoice in that which is revealed unto thee. And of the clans there are who deny some of it. Say: I am commanded only that I serve Allah and ascribe unto Him no partner. Unto Him I cry, and unto Him is my return

13:37.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ أَنزَلۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمًا عَرَبِيࣰّ اۚ وَلَئِنِ ٱتَّبَعۡتَ أَهۡوَآءَهُم بَعۡدَ مَا جَآءَكَ مِنَ ٱلۡعِلۡمِ مَا لَكَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ مِن وَلِيࣲّ وَلَا وَاقࣲ‏
13:37.en: Thus have We revealed it, a decisive utterance in Arabic; and if thou shouldst follow their desires after that which hath come unto thee of knowledge, then truly wouldst thou have from Allah no protecting friend nor defender

13:11.ar: لَهُۥ مُعَقِّبَٰتࣱ مِّنۢ بَيۡنِ يَدَيۡهِ وَمِنۡ خَلۡفِهِۦ يَحۡفَظُونَهُۥ مِنۡ أَمۡرِ ٱللَّهِۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوۡمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُواْ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمۡۗ وَإِذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِقَوۡمࣲ سُوٓءࣰ ا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُۥۚ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَالٍ
13:11.en: For him are angels ranged before him and behind him, who guard him by Allah's command. Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts; and if Allah willeth misfortune for a folk there is none that can repel it, nor have they a defender beside Him

5Cv_VtfJxjw.speaker: adnan
5Cv_VtfJxjw.speaker_note: his Ramadan weekend tafsir series of Surat Al-Ra'd at the Muslim Wellness Network, in his usual voice
5Cv_VtfJxjw.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Ra'd: Part 7
5Cv_VtfJxjw.one_line: Ra'd 32-37: the Quran makes people the miracle, Allah's delayed punishment, defining what a god is, and accepting revelation whole without picking and choosing.
5Cv_VtfJxjw.summary: Picking up after the verse on the Quran's power, he argues that Allah gave this ummah a book that turns its readers into the miracle, using Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a poor shepherd boy who became the scholar of an empire, as proof. Verse 32 reminds the Prophet that earlier messengers were mocked and their nations seized after a delay; this ummah will not face collective destruction, so the question is never when Allah will act but what we should do. Images of children pulled from rubble are a wake-up call about our own weakness, division and indifference. Verse 33 asks whether the One watching every soul equals idols, and he insists Muslims define the word god: omniscient and one by definition, never used loosely. The plotting of the disbelievers was made attractive to them, which he traces to the small inner urge to manipulate once one discovers influence. Allah misguides only on the basis of people's choices. Paradise is described with rivers flowing beneath it, a symbol of self-sufficiency. Believers rejoice at revelation while others reject parts of it; he calls for unconditional acceptance of the truth, warns that the Prophet was prepared years in advance not to compromise, and tells people to admit weakness rather than pick and choose.

outline.heading: Opening
The law of change: start with yourself
outline.gist: Recap of the surah's core law: the future will not differ unless we become different people, and no one is exempt from self-reflection.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Quran makes you the miracle
outline.gist: Instead of physical miracles, Allah gave a book that transforms those who carry it; zoom out to see what it did for the companions as a group.

outline.heading: Ibn Mas'ud: from shepherd boy to scholar of an empire
outline.gist: A poor, physically slight boy tending sheep became the revered scholar of Kufa; the Quran can do the same for those it touches.

outline.heading: Earlier messengers were mocked, then their nations seized
outline.gist: Allah delayed the mockers, then took them so completely that archaeologists struggle to piece together their story.

outline.heading: No collective punishment for this ummah
outline.gist: This ummah's story is told differently; punishment is deferred, so there is always a chance to fix things.

outline.heading: Yunus left out of love for his people
outline.gist: Prophets wanted more delay for their people; Yunus left without permission and his people gained another chance to repent.

outline.heading: Ask what you must do, not when Allah will act
outline.gist: Children pulled from rubble are Allah turning to us: a wake-up call about our weakness and division, and a lifelong question of how to help.

outline.heading: Is the One watching over every soul like the idols?
outline.gist: Allah supervises every soul in all it earns; the challenge to name and describe the partners they ascribe.

outline.heading: Define the word god before you use it
outline.gist: By definition a god is all-knowing and one; using the word loosely, as in mythology, leads people to take Allah lightly and worship Him poorly.

outline.heading: Plotting made attractive: the urge to manipulate
outline.gist: Everyone discovers some influence over others and feels the urge to use it; the Quran reduces huge evils to a small inner flaw like Iblis's arrogance.

outline.heading: Misguidance follows people's choices
outline.gist: Allah misguides on the basis of what people choose; liars and manipulators face punishment here and worse in the Hereafter.

outline.heading: Interlude
Punishment and reward always paired
outline.gist: Wherever the Quran mentions punishment it mentions reward; the comparison is repeated because people lose sight of it.

outline.heading: Rivers flowing beneath: self-sufficiency in Paradise
outline.gist: Water from one's own land symbolizes needing no one; its fruit and shade are continuous, physically and psychologically.

outline.heading: Those given the book rejoice at revelation
outline.gist: Two readings of 'those given the book': earlier scriptured peoples or the Muslims; here it is the believers celebrating each revelation.

outline.heading: Some factions find parts of it strange
outline.gist: The word means both rejecting and not recognizing; some truth feels hard to swallow because of the falsehood we have lived with.

outline.heading: Unconditional acceptance of the truth
outline.gist: Being Muslim means accepting the truth whether or not you agreed with it; serve Allah alone and return to Him.

outline.heading: An Arabic law for a people without law
outline.gist: Hukm here is law: tribal Arabs lived by breakable verbal agreements, so a binding law was new and some disliked it.

outline.heading: Pressure to compromise and follow their desires
outline.gist: Bringing truth means swimming upstream; the nobles asked him to separate them from the poor, and the verse forbids bending.

outline.heading: Prepared a decade before the Confederates
outline.gist: The word for factions was revealed in Makkah years before the Battle of the Trench, preparing him never to compromise to avoid it.

outline.heading: Do not pick and choose
outline.gist: Accept all of Islam; if you cannot practise some of it, admit weakness and ask for time, but never reject parts you dislike.

outline.heading: Outro

10:58.ar: قُلۡ بِفَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ وَبِرَحۡمَتِهِۦ فَبِذَٰلِكَ فَلۡيَفۡرَحُواْ هُوَ خَيۡرࣱ مِّمَّا يَجۡمَعُونَ
10:58.en: Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy: therein let them rejoice. It is better than what they hoard

73:1.en: O thou wrapped up in thy raiment

73:2.en: Keep vigil the night long, save a little

73:3.en: A half thereof, or abate a little thereof

73:4.ar: أَوۡ زِدۡ عَلَيۡهِ وَرَتِّلِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ تَرۡتِيلًا
73:4.en: Or add (a little) thereto - and chant the Qur'an in measure

73:5.ar: إِنَّا سَنُلۡقِي عَلَيۡكَ قَوۡلࣰ ا ثَقِيلًا
73:5.en: For we shall charge thee with a word of weight

73:6.ar: إِنَّ نَاشِئَةَ ٱلَّيۡلِ هِيَ أَشَدُّ وَطۡـࣰٔ ا وَأَقۡوَمُ قِيلًا
73:6.en: Lo! the vigil of the night is (a time) when impression is more keen and speech more certain

73:7.ar: إِنَّ لَكَ فِي ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبۡحࣰ ا طَوِيلࣰ ا
73:7.en: Lo! thou hast by day a chain of business

8:72.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَهَاجَرُواْ وَجَٰهَدُواْ بِأَمۡوَٰلِهِمۡ وَأَنفُسِهِمۡ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَاوَواْ وَّنَصَرُوٓاْ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ بَعۡضُهُمۡ أَوۡلِيَآءُ بَعۡضࣲۚ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَلَمۡ يُهَاجِرُواْ مَا لَكُم مِّن وَلَٰيَتِهِم مِّن شَيۡءٍ حَتَّىٰ يُهَاجِرُواْۚ وَإِنِ ٱسۡتَنصَرُوكُمۡ فِي ٱلدِّينِ فَعَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلنَّصۡرُ إِلَّا عَلَىٰ قَوۡمِۭ بَيۡنَكُمۡ وَبَيۡنَهُم مِّيثَٰقࣱۗ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ بَصِيرࣱ‏
8:72.en: Lo! those who believed and left their homes and strove with their wealth and their lives for the cause of Allah, and those who took them in and helped them: these are protecting friends one of another. And those who believed but did not leave their homes, ye have no duty to protect them till they leave their homes; but if they seek help from you in the matter of religion then it is your duty to help (them) except against a folk between whom and you there is a treaty. Allah is Seer of what ye do

8:73.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ بَعۡضُهُمۡ أَوۡلِيَآءُ بَعۡضٍۚ إِلَّا تَفۡعَلُوهُ تَكُن فِتۡنَةࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَفَسَادࣱ كَبِيرࣱ‏
8:73.en: And those who disbelieve are protectors one of another - If ye do not so, there will be confusion in the land, and great corruption

20:126.ar: قَالَ كَذَٰلِكَ أَتَتۡكَ ءَايَٰتُنَا فَنَسِيتَهَاۖ وَكَذَٰلِكَ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ تُنسَىٰ
20:126.en: He will say: So (it must be). Our revelations came unto thee but thou didst forget them. In like manner thou art forgotten this Day

SS42RR6G_RI.speaker: adnan
SS42RR6G_RI.speaker_note: tells his own story: born in Toronto, chose to live in Syria, forced to leave; refers to his priorities talk from last year
SS42RR6G_RI.title: Beyond Ramadan: What We Need to Do to Be Well
SS42RR6G_RI.one_line: After Ramadan, he argues the sign of acceptance is continuing the work outside the masjid, and calls people to commit to five community priorities that serve advocacy.
SS42RR6G_RI.summary: He opens on the Eid greeting: as a dua it is fine, but as a statement it is false, because the ummah is unwell, especially in the past six months. The time after Ramadan matters most. No deed can be proven accepted, but scholars agree the main sign is that worship continues and changes how one lives. Full masjids in the last ten nights mean nothing if life returns to normal, and Allah does not accept a religion split into rituals without standing for what is right. Just as night prayer prepared the Prophet for a heavy message, Ramadan is a launching pad and fuel for the real work outside the masjid. He revisits last year's five priorities for Muslims in the West (education, mentorship, outreach, centralized wealth and advocacy), now seeing advocacy as the goal the others serve. Born in Toronto and having chosen to live in Syria until forced out, he says the purpose of being here is to speak for those who have no voice. Gaza shows that money, not rights, buys a hearing, yet the community lacks willpower and organization, not resources. He asks everyone to commit to one or two fields they are suited to, and to treat the masjid as the place to regroup before the work outside.

outline.heading: Opening
Rejoice in Allah's bounty; we are not well
outline.gist: He recites 10:58 and says the Eid greeting is a fair dua but a false statement: the ummah and the community are very unwell, and these last six months have been the least well in a decade.

outline.heading: The accepted and the deprived
outline.gist: The time after Ramadan may matter most. Ibn Masud would ask who was accepted, to congratulate him, and who was deprived, to console him; every day without disobedience is Eid, and what we celebrate is the ability Allah gave us to fast, pray and recite.

outline.heading: Full masjids have no innate value
outline.gist: Allah calls His servants into His houses in Ramadan, but if packed masjids do not translate into worship afterwards, that is almost evidence the worship was not accepted.

outline.heading: No proof of acceptance, but one sign: continuing
outline.gist: No deed is ever provably accepted, since sincerity, commitment or humility may have been lacking, so we keep striving. The scholars nearly agree that the main sign of acceptance is continuing afterwards and letting it change your choices and direction.

outline.heading: Packed nights, then what? A compartmentalized deen
outline.gist: Every masjid fills in the last ten nights, with fifty rows and tears, but if it ends there the deeds may not reach the first heaven. Allah does not accept someone who takes the rituals and refuses to stand for what is right.

outline.heading: Night prayer as fuel for a heavy message
outline.gist: The Prophet was told to pray much of the night because he would carry a heavy word and the day is a long swim of work (73:1-7). Ramadan is that fuel for the real work, which happens outside the masjid doors.

outline.heading: Ramadan is a launching pad
outline.gist: The masjid and Ramadan train and energize you to carry the work outside; ending there is like taking a training course and never using it. Let the month shape your decisions afterwards.

outline.heading: We sail together or sink together
outline.gist: We do not exist as individuals in Allah's eyes; you belong to the Prophet's ummah whether you like it or not, and without living for that cause he does not see the value of the rituals.

outline.heading: Priority one: education
outline.gist: Last year he named five priorities for Muslims in the West and now sees them as one goal with four supports. The community must be educated academically and Islamically, with careers and influence and the knowledge to speak in the name of the deen.

outline.heading: Priority two: mentorship
outline.gist: The cause must be handed to the next generation and not die with you. That takes personal relationships and investing in younger people, with all the headaches that brings, and it is obligatory.

outline.heading: Priority three: outreach
outline.gist: Reach out not only to non-Muslims with dawah but to Muslims who never found their place in the masjid or did not grow up in it, to see how to serve them and their children.

outline.heading: Priority four: centralized wealth
outline.gist: Wealth is finite, so big financial decisions must serve the whole community, not a few elites, including ways to support those who want to marry, buy homes and start businesses.

outline.heading: Priority five: advocacy, and the verse of Al-Anfal
outline.gist: If your brothers ask for help you must give it; the disbelievers stand by one another, and failing to do so brings fitnah and great corruption on earth (8:72-73). After reassessing with others he found nothing to add to the five.

outline.heading: Interlude
Put yourselves to the challenge
outline.gist: If you believe Islam is more than rituals and zakah, choose a field and get involved so the effort is organized for the whole city, not only those who attend this masjid.

outline.heading: Advocacy: the one goal of our existence here
outline.gist: We carry a communal obligation to be the voice of the voiceless. In the Middle East governments slowly strip away Muslim identity, and most Muslims there, even weak in practice, long for Islam to fare better but have no voice.

outline.heading: Why would anyone leave? His own story
outline.gist: Having that right here brings the responsibility. Born in Toronto, he chose to live, study and marry in Syria and could not see why anyone would leave the ummah's needs there, until he was forced to leave or die. Now here, he must have a purpose beyond eating and drinking.

outline.heading: Every field serves advocacy
outline.gist: Being born here does not excuse anyone from having a purpose. Advocates must be well informed and confident, so education; advocacy is an art learned by observation, so mentorship; outreach multiplies the advocates.

outline.heading: Money speaks, not rights or blood
outline.gist: It is now shamefully clear that money, not human rights or blood, buys a hearing from corrupt politicians; 33,000 to 35,000 dead in Gaza mean nothing without it. We are not poor in numbers, youth, expertise or skills.

outline.heading: We lack willpower and organization
outline.gist: What we lack is willpower, organization and leadership; we are stuck in small, agenda-driven goals and silos. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not abandon him or fail to stand for his rights.

outline.heading: Abandon the wronged and Allah abandons you
outline.gist: Whoever supports someone whose rights are taken, Allah supports him when he needs it; whoever fails them, Allah lets him down when he needs someone to stand by him.

outline.heading: Gaza: a sign more glaring than the eclipse
outline.gist: Our signs came to you and you forgot them (20:126). People rushed to watch an eclipse, yet ignore a child eating grass and a mother mourning her baby: Allah is telling us to wake up. Let Ramadan turn your life around.

outline.heading: The masjid is where we regroup
outline.gist: Confidence in one's own acceptance is arrogance; the work happens outside. The masjid is where the exhausted and defeated come to find peace and support, regroup, debrief and remind themselves why, as the Prophet used it, before going back out.

outline.heading: Find what you can do
outline.gist: Work out what you are good at and interested in, whether education, mentorship, outreach, wealth or advocacy, and do something with your community so you can tell Allah you tried.

outline.heading: Real achievements, not new buildings
outline.gist: No one is proud of another masjid or Quran program, which run everywhere, even under bombing. Achievements in advocacy and in pushing back a racist, double-standard narrative would restore the community's morale and make people work harder.

outline.heading: Interlude
Dua from a sincere, focused heart
outline.gist: Millions made dua this Ramadan, but Allah accepts dua only from focused, sincere hearts, not distracted ones; live a life that reflects what you ask Him for.

outline.heading: Outro

bk4cpVO2ZVQ.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 27: Seventh Night of Tahajjud
bk4cpVO2ZVQ.one_line: How to ask Allah on the 27th night, His 'afw that erases a sin entirely, and the hard work of truly pardoning others.
bk4cpVO2ZVQ.summary: The first reminder is about how to make dua on this night. He asks people to sit before Allah with the manners of a sinner, to ask for what is best for them while trusting His wisdom over their own judgement, to speak to Him about their future, worries and hopes, and to keep returning to the plea for forgiveness. The second reminder explains the dua the Prophet taught Aisha for Laylat al-Qadr, asking Allah who loves to pardon to pardon us. Forgiveness can leave a deed on record to be discussed on the Day; 'afw wipes it away. He paints a scene: you rise from the grave anxious about one deed, take your book and hunt for it by the date you remember, but it is gone; you seek out the people you harmed to apologise, and they do not know what you are talking about. Pardoning others is the human side of this. He tells how pardoning someone who took everything from him was the hardest thing he ever did and took two years, because real pardon means never mentioning it again, restoring trust and helping the person when they need it.

outline.heading: Interlude
Ask for what is best, trusting His wisdom
outline.gist: Sit before Allah with the manners of a sinner and ask Him for what is best for you, trusting His wisdom more than your own judgement of what you need.

outline.heading: Tell Him about your future, worries and hopes
outline.gist: Speak to Allah about what you are worried about, what you care for and what you hope to achieve in your life.

outline.heading: Keep returning to asking forgiveness
outline.gist: Between these requests, keep repeating the plea to be forgiven, as the Prophet did, conscious of Allah's greatness.

outline.heading: Interlude
The dua of Laylat al-Qadr asks for 'afw
outline.gist: The Prophet taught Aisha to ask Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon; forgiveness can leave a deed to be discussed on the Day, while 'afw removes it.

outline.heading: Searching your book for the deed you feared
outline.gist: Picture rising from the grave worried about one deed, flipping to the day you remember committing it and finding nothing there, then searching again in frustration.

outline.heading: Even those you harmed do not remember
outline.gist: You go to the people you wronged to apologise before judgement and they ask what you are talking about; Allah's pardon makes it as if it never happened.

outline.heading: The hardest pardon he ever gave
outline.gist: Pardoning someone who mistreated him and took away everything, with no way to get his right back, was the most difficult thing he has done and took two years.

outline.heading: What pardoning someone really means
outline.gist: His first attempt failed, because pardon means never raising it again, in private or public, restoring trust and supporting the person when they need it; letting go hurts like nothing else.

outline.heading: Interlude

GAL5PDlmc14.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 27: Appreciations
GAL5PDlmc14.one_line: A brief appreciation of the young men who led the Ramadan prayers, and why handing the baton to the next generation matters.
GAL5PDlmc14.summary: In this short talk on the twenty-seventh night he explains why the night prayers are shared among young reciters instead of being led by him alone. Running it himself would be easy and quicker, he says, but giving young men the chance encourages them and also inspires the even younger generation watching them, and there is no future for the work unless the baton is handed down. He adds that no one can carry this kind of work without supportive companions who keep helping and keep working with the youth. He then honours the core group who led most of the prayers that month, as well as those given a few slots to encourage them to work hard. He prays that Allah makes them ambassadors of the Quran, increases their love of it, lets them spread it among people, and brings newer and younger people to join every year, and he asks the congregation to listen to the new reciters and make dua for them.

H7GI7PcY1Eg.speaker: adnan
H7GI7PcY1Eg.speaker_note: says these are the same three reminders he gives every year; same voice and themes as his other Ramadan khutbahs
H7GI7PcY1Eg.title: Final Three Ramadan Reminders
H7GI7PcY1Eg.one_line: Three end-of-Ramadan reminders: it is not over until it is over, seek Allah's pardon by pardoning others, and treat Ramadan as a launching pad.
H7GI7PcY1Eg.summary: On the 26th day of Ramadan he offers the three reminders he repeats each year. First, it is not over until it is over: as long as a second remains there is hope, so renew your intention. The Prophet modeled this when, rejected by 26 tribes, he stayed at Mina until the last hour of the last day of Tashreeq and met the six young men from Yathrib. Second, the 27th night, culturally and in scholarship, is the night of pardon. He distinguishes forgiveness, where a sin stays in your record marked forgiven, from pardon, where it is erased so even the recording angel and the person harmed forget it. To receive that, pardon others fully and restore trust, as Umar did publicly before this night; Allah will not let His servant be more generous than Him. Third, full masjids have no value in themselves. Prayer is fuel, as night prayer was for the Prophet's heavy message, and the masjid is where Islam is trained, not where it is practised. What matters is who keeps coming, learns, organizes and advocates afterwards. He then calls the 170-plus days of Gaza a wake-up call and asks each listener to be among the handful in every masjid who live differently.

outline.heading: Opening
Reminder one: it is not over until it is over
outline.gist: Allah calls the fast a few numbered days, and they are ending. While even a second remains, renew your intention and push for what you hoped for: forgiveness, freedom from punishment, more good deeds, an answered dua.

outline.heading: The Prophet at Mina until the last hour
outline.gist: In the tenth year, seeking a tribe to protect him, he was rejected by 26 tribes. Most pilgrims left Mina after two days, but he stayed into the third, and at its last hour in the farthest corner of Mina he met six young men from Yathrib.

outline.heading: Hope until the last moment
outline.gist: The eldest of the six was 21, and the rest is history. On the 26th day, with Ramadan running to 30, there is still hope to keep your promise to Allah and see Him keep His.

outline.heading: Interlude
Reminder two: the 27th night, the night of pardon
outline.gist: The night moves each year, but the 27th holds a cultural and scholarly place in the ummah as the night of 'afw, when you can hope Allah will pardon you.

outline.heading: Forgiveness keeps the record; pardon erases it
outline.gist: A forgiven sin stays in your book, marked forgiven, and you must read it back. A pardoned sin is gone: the angel who wrote it and the person you harmed do not recall it, and you search for the one thing you feared.

outline.heading: As if it never happened
outline.gist: Allah tells you only He and you know of it, and that He will make you forget it too, so it is not as if it did not happen but it did not happen. Receiving that requires pardoning others.

outline.heading: Umar pardons everyone before this night
outline.gist: Pardon means turning the page: never raising the wrong again and restoring trust, moving from negative not to neutral but to high positive. Umar told the people of Madinah that he pardoned them all, asked them to do the same, then asked Allah to pardon him.

outline.heading: Allah will not be outdone in generosity
outline.gist: Pardoning those who wronged you may be the hardest thing you ever do, though it needs no physical effort. Allah refuses to let His servant be more generous than Him: pardon and you will be pardoned.

outline.heading: Interlude
Reminder three: full masjids are not the goal
outline.gist: Packed masjids have no value in themselves; tens of thousands pray in masjids across the Muslim world. Numbers mean nothing unless Ramadan launches people into changed lives.

outline.heading: Prayer is fuel for work outside
outline.gist: The ummah is not fixed by praying and making dua all night. Prayer refuels people so they go out and make a difference, and come back when they tire; he was surprised the opposite belief exists.

outline.heading: Night prayer for a heavy message (73:5-7)
outline.gist: Allah told the Prophet a heavy word was coming, that night prayer is strongest, and that by day he would have a long swim among problems and people. Without strong spirituality the outside work cannot be done.

outline.heading: Where Islam is trained, not practised
outline.gist: Quantity means nothing; prayer must translate into change outside. The masjid nurtures Islam and launches people into the world where it is practised. Dua shows Allah we care, but means little without the work.

outline.heading: What happened afterwards?
outline.gist: How many kept coming, educated themselves, organized, or took up outreach, mentorship or advocacy? Prayer is not the work; it is Allah's door opened so you taste the beauty of connection and spend your life working for Him.

outline.heading: Not about numbers
outline.gist: Otherwise next year is a replica: full masjids, proud photos on social media, nothing changed. If you do not move forward you regress, and the Prophet and the Quran repeat that numbers do not count.

outline.heading: Ramadan ends, the relationship begins
outline.gist: What matters is quality: dedication, grit, resilience. Ramadan is almost over, but your relationship with Allah is just starting; that beginning is what you celebrate.

outline.heading: Celebrate by giving
outline.gist: Start the new life by giving from what you have, even a little, to those without enough to eat. Do not let the month's purpose be defeated the moment it ends.

outline.heading: Do not walk away from an open door
outline.gist: Allah opened His doors and put something in your heart you never felt before; turning your back afterwards is not fair. Ramadan is where we train for who we must be outside the masjid.

outline.heading: Interlude
Make sure it never happens again
outline.gist: After 170-plus days of brutality in Gaza documented moment by moment, we cannot stop it immediately, but we have the tools to ensure it is not forgotten or repeated, unlike the decades we spent looking away.

outline.heading: If this does not wake us, nothing will
outline.gist: We book vacations and focus on what we buy next. If these six months do not change how he and his listeners see the world and their role in it, nothing will.

outline.heading: The witness and the witnessed (85:3)
outline.gist: Children brought lifeless to emergency rooms, eating grass from hunger, families buried under their homes: you cannot see this and act as if you did not. A handful of changed people in every masjid would transform the ummah; be among them.

outline.heading: Outro

h7mmYqMPUO0.speaker: adnan
h7mmYqMPUO0.speaker_note: Final night of his Ramadan 2024 Quranic Reflections series, leading the khatm
h7mmYqMPUO0.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 29: Quranic Reflections (Al-Fajr to An-Nas)
h7mmYqMPUO0.one_line: Juz Amma as faith, choice, a toolkit and concentrated values; living for the real life, ease within hardship, the scales, prayer that withholds aid, and the two refuges.
h7mmYqMPUO0.summary: On the final night he maps Juz Amma: the three elements of faith, the sacred and accountable nature of choice, a toolkit for life that includes the right lens on blessings and trials and consistency of values at one's lowest and highest points, and finally short surahs that work like concentrated pills of value, which is why children memorise them and why parents should learn their meanings to teach them. From al-Fajr he describes the regret of one who realises too late that the Hereafter is real life, noting that this world is not built for reclining. Ash-Sharh teaches that worry must not cripple you: ease comes with hardship, not after it, so look for it, focus on your task and turn to Allah. Al-Qari'ah shatters status, degrees and reputation until only the weight of the scales matters, so make every achievement count there. Al-Ma'un, read without and then with its last verse, shows that perfecting prayer is not enough while withholding help others need, since the ruling on giving shifts with context. Al-Falaq and an-Nas teach refuge from outside harm and from becoming a source of harm by acting on whispers. He closes by urging that Ramadan's clarity become a long-term change in how people live outside the masjid.

outline.heading: Opening
Juz Amma: what most people memorise as children
outline.gist: Everyone should know this juz, and the ambitious should work toward the whole Mufassal; it divides into four groups of surahs.

outline.heading: First group: three components of faith
outline.gist: What Allah wants, what you need to reach it, and your ethical standard.

outline.heading: Second group: the sanctity of choice
outline.gist: Choice is God-given and no one may take it, yet it is recorded, accountable and narrow, and doing nothing is also a choice; these surahs deserve recitation with reflection.

outline.heading: Why children start with Juz Amma
outline.gist: A child who understands it leaves with clarity about the deen and themselves: few rulings but many values and principles.

outline.heading: Third group: a toolkit for life
outline.gist: Tools to pull out in life's ups and downs: exalting Allah and perseverance among them.

outline.heading: Al-Fajr: the right lens
outline.gist: Seeing every good as Allah's pleasure and every hardship as His wrath is delusion; all of it is a test whose outcome depends on your response.

outline.heading: Consistent values at the lowest and highest points
outline.gist: Values cannot be selective; your darkest moment and your peak are when you are watched under a magnifying glass, since near neutral it is easy to be yourself.

outline.heading: Purifying the self
outline.gist: Self-awareness and self-accountability complete the toolkit.

outline.heading: A toolkit worth more than anything you buy
outline.gist: We use these words without understanding them; practising them takes a lifelong journey of education.

outline.heading: Interlude
Fourth group: surahs like concentrated pills
outline.gist: Al-Baqarah is about 150 times the length of the shortest surah, yet each is a full surah because the short ones concentrate equally profound teaching, giving access to Allah's wisdom even without the whole Quran.

outline.heading: Learn their meanings to teach your children
outline.gist: Each surah carries a value for life, such as how to respond when mocked or bullied, what to do in hardship, or what a good person is; study them so you can explain them to your children.

outline.heading: The companion who loved al-Ikhlas
outline.gist: Repeating the same short surahs is fine if you understand and enjoy their meaning; a companion recited al-Ikhlas in every rakah because it describes the Most Merciful, and the Prophet approved.

outline.heading: Interlude
I wish I had sent something ahead
outline.gist: At the end a person realises how short this existence was and how vast the coming one is, and wishes he had invested in it.

outline.heading: Death is the door to real life
outline.gist: Death is a transition to what Allah calls true life; this life is beautiful but bounded by pain, failure and limits, and those who built only here find nothing there.

outline.heading: Not designed for reclining
outline.gist: When young and healthy you are broke and unheard; by the time you have wealth, wisdom and status your body is failing, so even without revelation life is plainly not built to settle into.

outline.heading: Green, yellow, then gone
outline.gist: Like plants after rain we flourish and wither; on that Day no one punishes or binds as Allah does.

outline.heading: Worry, but not to the point of dysfunction
outline.gist: Some concern for the future is healthy; pathological worry cripples, and the surah tells the Prophet to stop worrying.

outline.heading: Did We not expand your chest?
outline.gist: The surah opens mid-conversation, answering the Prophet's anxiety about whether he was succeeding; Allah eased his heart, lifted his burden and raised his mention.

outline.heading: With hardship, not after it
outline.gist: Ease comes with the difficulty, not after it; some hardships last to the end of life, but there is always enough ease within them to function and persevere if you look for it.

outline.heading: Stop rehearsing what-ifs
outline.gist: The darkness may not lift, but you will get through; do not torment yourself over scenarios you cannot control, as parents often do for their children.

outline.heading: Do your task, then strive again
outline.gist: Leave what you cannot change, focus on the job at hand, then keep going and draw closer to Allah.

outline.heading: Al-Qari'ah: the blow that changes everything
outline.gist: Qar' is a strike so hard it changes a thing's nature; on that Day the laws of the universe and of human life no longer apply.

outline.heading: Status, degrees and connections shatter
outline.gist: Wealth, networks, power and the letters before and after your name defined you here; the soul is not ready to lose them all at once.

outline.heading: Only the weight of the scales remains
outline.gist: Heavy scales mean a pleasing life; light ones cannot be made up for with money, certificates or status.

outline.heading: People's testimony carries no weight
outline.gist: Even if everyone vouched for him it would change nothing; only what Allah knows and what you know about yourself matters.

outline.heading: The big man with no weight
outline.gist: The Prophet described a huge man who jumps into his own scale to weigh it down and weighs nothing; weight in the sense of standing means nothing there.

outline.heading: Achieve, but make it weigh on the scale
outline.gist: Gain wealth, study and build networks, but if none of it makes your scale heavier it was a waste of time.

outline.heading: Read al-Ma'un without its last verse
outline.gist: The surah is named for its final word; read it first without the last verse to see why.

outline.heading: The one who denies the deen
outline.gist: Those who reject what they know is true mistreat the orphan and do not urge feeding the needy: the prototype Allah rejects.

outline.heading: Woe to those who pray
outline.gist: Prayer is usually praised, yet here those who neglect it physically and spiritually and pray to be seen are warned; ending there would mean simply perfecting your prayer.

outline.heading: Withholding aid: piety is never one-dimensional
outline.gist: The surah ends with those who withhold help; nowhere does the Quran accept correct theology and rituals without worship that benefits people.

outline.heading: The ruling on giving shifts with context
outline.gist: Charity is sunnah by default, forbidden when you owe a creditor waiting to be paid, and obligatory when someone starves beside you; ma'un is aid someone is asking for.

outline.heading: We did not pray, and we did not feed the needy
outline.gist: Those in the depth of Hell name both failures together, echoing al-Ma'un: prayer without helping those in need does not save.

outline.heading: Interlude
Two final refuges: from without and from within
outline.gist: The Quran ends with refuge from harm that comes from outside and harm that comes from inside; al-Falaq begins with the Lord of creation bursting into existence.

outline.heading: Al-Falaq: four external evils
outline.gist: Refuge from the evil of all creation, from darkness covering what light remains, from those who put obstacles in your way, and from envy in another's heart.

outline.heading: Praised once, then three times
outline.gist: Al-Falaq praises Allah once because external evils are easy for Him to brush away; an-Nas praises Him three times because the harm it addresses is harder.

outline.heading: Lord, King and God against the whisperer
outline.gist: All three relationships with Allah are invoked against the hidden whisperer who plants small thoughts in the chest, whether jinn or human.

outline.heading: The real harm is the harm that comes from you
outline.gist: A whisper or a bad suggestion does not harm you; harm happens when you accept it and act on it, becoming a source of harm to the world.

outline.heading: Refuge as the key to living the Quran
outline.gist: To practise the whole book and walk with its guidance, first seek refuge in Allah from external and internal harm.

outline.heading: Interlude
What changes the world is what happens outside the masjid
outline.gist: Full masjids are not the measure; the clarity and love Allah gives in Ramadan must translate into how you live every day.

outline.heading: Make Ramadan a long-term plan
outline.gist: Without a life-changing plan Ramadan's benefit is limited; the ummah was better off a century ago but is more aware today, which gives him hope.

outline.heading: Outro

TbJn5nqkW5s.speaker: adnan
TbJn5nqkW5s.speaker_note: Ramadan post-Fajr series; refers back to the five fields for Muslims in the West he presented the previous year
TbJn5nqkW5s.title: End of Ramadan Reflections
TbJn5nqkW5s.one_line: Packed masjids mean nothing unless Ramadan launches each Muslim into a lifelong role serving an ummah that is starving and oppressed.
TbJn5nqkW5s.summary: He closes Ramadan with a pointed question: what is the value of masjids filled with thousands every night when Muslims a day's travel away are starving? The proof that Ramadan was accepted is what a person does once it ends. He recalls that the Prophet's first act in Medina was to build a very simple masjid, a place where the companions took their dose of faith and then went out to build a nation. Today the ummah fills buildings and posts photos of the crowds, which he likens to the foam of the flood: plenty of it, no weight. Rebuilding what took centuries to tear down needs grit and a lifetime of dedication. Each person should look at where Allah has placed them, find their own piece of the mosaic by trial and error, and carry the ummah instead of being carried by it. He revisits his five fields for Muslims in the West: education, mentorship, dawah, community finance and advocacy, tying the last to the Gaza genocide and the community's disorganization. Like the companions who left the joy of the first Ramadan to face the enemy at Badr, worship must become fuel for standing up for what is right, done together with the community. The masjid is where the work begins, and the place to return to for strength.

outline.heading: Opening
What is the point of packed masjids?
outline.gist: Masjids across the Muslim world are full every night of Ramadan while fellow Muslims starve less than a day's travel away.

outline.heading: Accepted Ramadan shows in what comes after
outline.gist: The way to know Ramadan was accepted is how you behave once it is over; full masjids must turn into meaningful action for the ummah.

outline.heading: The masjid as a starting point
outline.gist: The Prophet's first masjid in Medina was barely a building, yet the companions drew their faith there and used it to build a nation. Today we fill masjids and share photos of the crowds without knowing what comes next.

outline.heading: Foam of the flood: numbers without weight
outline.gist: Large crowds frighten him because they resemble the Prophet's warning about foam. A masjid that does not launch people into action is not doing its job.

outline.heading: Rebuilding takes a lifetime of grit
outline.gist: The ummah was built on sweat, tears and blood over years and has been torn down over centuries; rebuilding needs resilient, fully dedicated people.

outline.heading: Work where Allah placed you
outline.gist: Do not waste time on questions you cannot answer; look at where you are, the people around you and your community, and work there.

outline.heading: Carry the ummah or become dead weight
outline.gist: If you are not carrying the ummah, it is carrying you. Ramadan lasts a month so that you have time to reflect and make that decision as a turning point.

outline.heading: Find your piece of the mosaic
outline.gist: Each person is a small piece of a vast mosaic; nobody can dictate your role, so try things until you find what you are good at and keep doing it until you meet Allah.

outline.heading: Five fields for Muslims in the West: education
outline.gist: After years of thought he still holds to five fields; the first, knowledge, protects the community from worshipping Allah ignorantly.

outline.heading: Five fields: mentorship
outline.gist: Without mentorship the next generation will not know its deen or keep its identity, and the community may vanish within decades.

outline.heading: Five fields: dawah to lost Muslims and to non-Muslims
outline.gist: Everyone has relatives and friends who never come to the masjid; if guidance is a blessing we should care about them, and compassion should extend to non-Muslims too.

outline.heading: Five fields: community finance
outline.gist: A young, working community has real wealth; it must be pooled and spent on real needs instead of being drained into masjids nobody needs.

outline.heading: Five fields: advocacy and the Gaza genocide
outline.gist: He did not foresee a six-month genocide in the Holy Land. People there are bombed and starved because the ummah is weak, leaderless and disorganized; organized communities with wealth and advocates could stop it.

outline.heading: Are rituals accepted without our central role?
outline.gist: He sounds an alarm: we cannot expect Allah to accept rituals alone while we abandon our core duty to stand against wrong.

outline.heading: Badr in the first Ramadan: the struggle is outside
outline.gist: The companions were enjoying the first Ramadan with the Prophet, yet went out to face the strongest army in the land; worship is fuel for standing up for what is right.

outline.heading: Work as part of a community
outline.gist: You are part of a group even if you dislike it, and must work with it; the killing has not stopped and may get worse, which should wake us up.

outline.heading: Choose a field and organize
outline.gist: Pick one or two of the five fields, or propose another, so people who care about the same work can form ongoing efforts; the ummah's potential depends on willingness to commit for life.

outline.heading: Return to the masjid to refuel
outline.gist: When tired, defeated or empty, come back to the masjid for strength and then face the world again; it is where things begin, not where they end.

outline.heading: Outro

y5gW6Zq0Xo0.title: Reduced Concepts, Episode 7: Ethics, Taqwa, Tawakkul and Jumuah
y5gW6Zq0Xo0.one_line: Series finale on concepts reduced to empty shells: ethics must be consistent, taqwa is preventive decision-making, tawakkul follows full effort, and Jumuah is leadership.
y5gW6Zq0Xo0.summary: Closing his Reduced Concepts series, a Sunday lecture rather than a khutbah, he asks listeners to keep reassessing inherited values so they do not become empty shells. Ethics differ from other concepts: whatever they are reduced to, from fake smiles to elitism, backfires, and false humility is worse than open pride. His rule is that an ethic is either consistent or non-existent, shown in how you treat those who can do nothing for you. He draws on the Prophet's gentleness with Bedouins, Surah al-Balad's call to feed the hungry when you are hungry yourself, Khadijah's description of the Prophet, and Yusuf's sameness in the well, prison and palace, and he condemns community circles that court only doctors and the wealthy. Taqwa is a preventive system: before every decision ask whether it will cause harm or displease Allah, like cancer screening versus costly late treatment, or Abu Hanifa's students ruling on cases before they arose; real tawbah means preventing a repeat. Tawakkul comes from understanding Allah's will, makes people bold, and applies only after full effort. Finally, Jumuah has been reduced to fundraising appeals and notices, though it was once the leader's weekly address; he calls for a leadership committee, qualified speakers and unified messaging across the city, drawing on Surah al-Jumuah's image of a donkey carrying books.

outline.heading: Why keep reassessing inherited concepts
outline.gist: Teachings preached without their essence stop helping people, especially the young, and they walk away; the companions felt Islam's difference in their own lives right away.

outline.heading: Whatever ethics are reduced to backfires
outline.gist: Unlike the earlier concepts, anything ethics are reduced to becomes a problem: empty smiles, rude 'haram police', mutual flattery with no honest feedback, elitism. Ethics are hard to judge inside the masjid, where everyone is on best behaviour.

outline.heading: False humility is worse than open pride
outline.gist: Calling yourself humble means you already see yourself above others and then claim moral credit for stooping: two faults plus a lie, where open pride is one fault that can be identified and fixed.

outline.heading: Consistent or non-existent
outline.gist: An ethic is always there or it is not there at all: arrogance towards one person makes you arrogant (oppressors are a separate discussion), and generosity or kindness that depends on circumstances or people is not an ethic.

outline.heading: Feed the hungry when you are hungry
outline.gist: Surah al-Balad came to the Prophet after Taif, at the worst moment of his life, and told him to free slaves and feed the hungry on a day of hunger: ethics hold even at your lowest point.

outline.heading: True colours show with those who can do nothing for you
outline.gist: Politicians help people for the image; the test is how you treat someone whose help adds nothing to you, not even reputation. Seeing yourself honestly there is an ugly but necessary mirror.

outline.heading: The Prophet with the despised Bedouins
outline.gist: The Bedouins had no status, wealth or manners and nothing to offer, yet he was never more tender: he held people back from the man who twisted his cloak, gave him more until he was pleased, likened himself to a man calming a runaway camel, and was gentle with the man who urinated in the masjid.

outline.heading: Elderly servant women and small children
outline.gist: Nameless elderly servant women held him for an hour or two after prayer with their problems, and young children took his hand to help with errands, and he went.

outline.heading: Selective behaviour is not an ethic
outline.gist: Treating someone with nothing to offer differently from others is a selective choice of behaviour; a real ethic defines you and never flips into its opposite, while faked humility is a play to win people over.

outline.heading: Ethics removed from finance and politics
outline.gist: Societies have openly stopped expecting leaders to be ethical, then vote for them out of desperation and hope the country will work.

outline.heading: Elitism: courting doctors and the wealthy
outline.gist: Showing warmth only to physicians, engineers, lawyers, PhDs or the rich and ignoring everyone else is one of the lowest behaviours and the exact opposite of ethics; prophets were surrounded by the weak.

outline.heading: His teacher on the baraka of welcoming the poor
outline.gist: An elderly teacher in Syria who had never heard of Canada said America was given baraka for its founding promise to take in the poor and needy; Muslims lost it by becoming elitist, with community circles of doctors and not one cab driver.

outline.heading: Khadijah: his ethics before prophethood
outline.gist: When he came down from the cave afraid, Khadijah told him Allah would never disgrace him because he cared for the destitute and carried those who could not carry themselves; that consistency is why he was chosen.

outline.heading: Yusuf the same in the well, prison and palace
outline.gist: Through every rise and fall Yusuf kept the same values, began dawah on his first day in prison, and chose years in jail over a sin no one would have punished him for.

outline.heading: Taqwa: one question before every decision
outline.gist: Taqwa has become an undefined pious word, but it is a proactive system rooted in protection and prevention: before any act or word, ask whether it will cause harm in the short or long term, and if so do not do it.

outline.heading: Oncology: prevention versus fourth-line drugs
outline.gist: The real corruption in cancer care is that almost nothing is invested in screening and prevention while billions go to fourth-line drugs buying months; public funding for prevention, like mammograms, does far more.

outline.heading: Thinking ahead: Abu Hanifa and prayer in flight
outline.gist: Muslims should live and organize ahead of problems instead of running behind them. Abu Hanifa's circle, having answered every current question, ruled on praying while standing on something not connected to the earth, so the fatwa was ready when planes came.

outline.heading: Avoid what displeases Allah; most of life is neutral
outline.gist: The taqwa question is whether an act displeases Allah, not whether it pleases Him, which is a higher level. Most choices are neutral and open; Allah is displeased by harm to yourself or others.

outline.heading: Real tawbah prevents the repeat
outline.gist: Saying 'I won't do it again' while changing nothing is a bet anyone would take against you; tawbah means setting up a way to prevent the sin from recurring.

outline.heading: Communal taqwa: the same problems for 50 years
outline.gist: Every masjid in the world has the same struggles (politics, old against young, buildings over people) because communities react instead of preventing. Start from avoiding Jahannam, the greatest harm, and work backwards.

outline.heading: Tawakkul, the fruit of understanding Allah's will
outline.gist: Tawakkul has been reduced to an excuse for being unprepared, but it grows from understanding Allah's will and makes a person calmer, more resilient and bolder than others.

outline.heading: The trustee contract: full effort, then acceptance
outline.gist: Once you take Allah as your trustee, you exhaust every resource and make sound decisions, then accept whatever result He gives and reassess; this is what lets people take calculated risks on uncharted ventures.

outline.heading: Tawakkul is for the student who studied
outline.gist: Students invoke tawakkul when they have not prepared; it belongs to the one who knows the syllabus, because even full preparation can fail and the result is in Allah's hands.

outline.heading: Effort is Allah's law; undeserved success is a warning
outline.gist: Succeeding with no effort over someone who worked day and night would mean Allah breaking His own laws; a little effort will not reverse 300 years of decline. When success comes without effort, it is a lifeline to wake up, not a reward.

outline.heading: Jumuah reduced to fundraising appeals
outline.gist: Friday prayer has become a slot for donation drives and lists of notices, when it was the community's weekly gathering where its leader addressed next steps, failures and successes.

outline.heading: Khalid ibn al-Walid on the minbar
outline.gist: On campaigns Khalid, who accepted Islam late and knew little Quran, gave the khutbah and led the prayer although far more learned companions were with him, because Jumuah belongs to the leader, as is well established.

outline.heading: The minbar belongs to the leader
outline.gist: A speaker with no decision-making weight leaves a dysfunctional community; the leader should be on the minbar after consulting scholars, or the khatib should speak on his behalf, as he himself once did.

outline.heading: No leadership: no direction, no accountability
outline.gist: Without leadership a community runs in circles like a headless chicken, never learning which direction fails, with no end goal beyond bringing people to Allah although Islam aims at justice and a fair life; no one is responsible, and he has no authority himself.

outline.heading: One message across the city
outline.gist: A Jumuah is only as valuable as the leadership behind it; if every khatib addressed the same priority in his own words and money went in one direction, a united, diverse community could finally achieve something tangible.

outline.heading: A weekly gathering that still draws people, for now
outline.gist: Jumuah draws about ten times the daily congregation across the city with no effort because Allah made it obligatory; the Prophet led through it, but if it keeps being mistreated attendance will fade like Sunday church.

outline.heading: A leadership committee and verified speakers
outline.gist: He proposes a committee of board heads that sets direction and an imam council that verifies who speaks; his own permission came in supervised stages over about 20 years, while today anyone puts on a hat and gives khutbah, which is fine only in schools and universities.

outline.heading: The donkey carrying books
outline.gist: Surah al-Jumuah, which speaks of the prophets' mission and commands Jumuah, likens those who carried the Torah without living it to a donkey carrying books: the image behind the whole series, as we carry salah without embracing its value.

outline.heading: Ethical leadership moves people; regimes fear Jumuah
outline.gist: Value-driven leadership inspires people to change, and in the West only egos and politics stand in the way; regimes in the Middle East regulate Jumuah and jail outspoken khatibs because they know its power.

outline.heading: The Syrian preacher jailed every month
outline.gist: A preacher in the city where he studied for exams spoke fluently for a full hour, filled the streets an hour early, woke sleepers by striking the minbar, and went to jail for a few days every month, yet moved people.

outline.heading: Restore the essence of our concepts
outline.gist: A properly led and planned Jumuah can move a society; perhaps the public will press institutions to work together. Analyze your own values for anything reduced to a shell, relearn it and change, because finding our way back means restoring their meaning.

outline.heading: Outro

IHNsEg-8Ekk.speaker: adnan
IHNsEg-8Ekk.speaker_note: Sheikh Adnan's own Ramadan series Reduced Concepts, episode six; refers to his Quran teaching and hospital work
IHNsEg-8Ekk.title: Reduced Concepts: The Quran, Tazkiyah and Good Deeds
IHNsEg-8Ekk.one_line: How three core concepts have shrunk: the Quran to blessings and recitation, tazkiyah to rituals and passivity (with a careful account of bid'ah), and good deeds to rituals.
IHNsEg-8Ekk.summary: Continuing his series on concepts Muslims have narrowed, the sheikh takes three. The Quran, the Prophet's main legacy, has been reduced to a token of blessing, funeral recitation, memorisation without understanding and ruqyah. None of these is wrong, but the companions learned ten verses at a time and applied them to themselves, and the Prophet warned of reciters whose reading does not pass their throats. He describes Quran classes as a hook for mentorship, and tells people to attend lessons rather than treat imams as an on-call question service. Tazkiyah, the third part of the religion in the hadith of Jibril (ihsan), has been reduced to singing, blind obedience to a sheikh, passive asceticism and neglect of law. Its real work is understanding the nafs that steers us, refusing to answer I don't know when asked why we act, and keeping the heart with Allah rather than fighting over details of posture. He then defines bid'ah: a newly invented religious practice with no general or specific basis, claimed equal to Allah's law, typically exaggerating worship. Only scholars should use the word; new services such as public dua or communal recitation are not bid'ah. Finally, a good deed (salih) is a functional one: today that means working for the state of the ummah and investing in people, not just building masajid.

outline.heading: Opening
The Quran is what the Prophet truly left us
outline.gist: Most of his effort went into preserving and teaching the Quran; neglecting its meaning is turning our backs on his legacy.

outline.heading: Reduced to a token of blessing
outline.gist: Expensive mushafs on display and in cars carry baraka, but not looking into what it teaches misses the point.

outline.heading: Followers of a book they have never read
outline.gist: Someone committed to a misunderstood faith is harder to help than someone who knows nothing; most misconceptions come from not reading the Quran in depth.

outline.heading: Reduced to funerals: tie it to joy instead
outline.gist: If the Quran only evokes death and hospital rooms the association turns negative; the old advice was to link each new chapter of life with a surah.

outline.heading: Reduced to memorisation and recitation
outline.gist: If pronunciation is the whole focus, meaning and practice are lost, like the reciters the Prophet warned of whose reading does not pass their throats.

outline.heading: Scholars who opposed teaching children to memorise
outline.gist: Many of his teachers felt memorisation should wait until maturity so the sanctity is felt; he now sees some merit in that view.

outline.heading: Quran classes as the easiest hook
outline.gist: Recitation programs bring people into the masjid when other courses draw ten people; memorisation is never the end goal.

outline.heading: Imams are not a personal question service
outline.gist: People skip lessons, then send urgent messages; when teaching is offered, attending is an obligation.

outline.heading: Memorisation is a means to mentorship
outline.gist: Teaching children Quran is about connecting them to Islam and guiding their lives.

outline.heading: Reduced to ruqyah
outline.gist: Reading only when afraid of envy or harm, then shelving the book; he recites over his children daily.

outline.heading: Knowledge remains while understanding disappears
outline.gist: The Prophet said knowledge is taken by the death of scholars: billions of mushafs, few who understand.

outline.heading: Each generation should know more than the last
outline.gist: A scholar's death leaves a gap unless students surpass him; learn while teachers are alive.

outline.heading: Ten verses at a time, applied to yourself
outline.gist: The companions practised before moving on; verses about hypocrites and enemies are warnings to reflect on yourself, not to project on others.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah reduced to singing and festivity
outline.gist: Purifying the self is central to the deen, but reducing it to nashid and celebration makes it seem without substance.

outline.heading: Reduced to blind obedience, yet a guide is needed
outline.gist: Obeying a sheikh teaches humility and you cannot travel this road without a guide, but tazkiyah is more than following.

outline.heading: Reduced to passive asceticism
outline.gist: For centuries people of tazkiyah withdrew from wealth and power, leaving them to those who ignore God, and Islam fizzled.

outline.heading: Abu Hanifah: ascetic and wealthy
outline.gist: A silk merchant who lived simply and paid the poor young Abu Yusuf a salary to study, producing a chief judge.

outline.heading: Reduced to neglect of law; the hadith of Jibril
outline.gist: Ignoring evidence makes tazkiyah unattractive; Jibril asked about islam, iman and ihsan as three equal parts.

outline.heading: Ihsan: the third third of Islam
outline.gist: Practice, theology and the inner discipline that replaces vanity, envy and laziness with humility, love and resilience.

outline.heading: Worship Allah as though you see Him
outline.gist: Everything else in closeness has been reached except seeing Him; this part of the hadith is almost never taught.

outline.heading: Where tasawwuf came from
outline.gist: From simple wool garments of people who cared little for the world, studied during Islam's golden age, not its decline.

outline.heading: The fake steering wheel
outline.gist: You know something is wrong and do it anyway because the nafs is driving and lets you believe you are in control.

outline.heading: Explaining laziness to an alien
outline.gist: Wanting to act, being able to, and still not doing it makes no sense until you understand the self.

outline.heading: Never answer I don't know
outline.gist: The first lesson of tazkiyah: an adult must find the real reason he does or does not act.

outline.heading: Overcompensating with physical details
outline.gist: When salah's spirit is empty people fight over finger movements and heels or toes, details the scholars differed on.

outline.heading: Hands in your pockets, heart with Allah
outline.gist: An early scholar asked about hand placement in prayer reminded the youths that without the heart with Allah nothing else matters.

outline.heading: The nafs: best ally, worst enemy, only thing you control
outline.gist: The nafs keeps your eyes on others' faults; look inward, where the answer to your struggles lies.

outline.heading: Bid'ah is a word for scholars
outline.gist: Calling something bid'ah is a grave accusation, like saying someone is headed for the Fire; students should not use it.

outline.heading: Why bid'ah matters and what it means
outline.gist: It guards the deen's boundaries, but it means a new matter with no general or specific basis in the law, not anything the Prophet did not do.

outline.heading: Two scholarly views on good and bad innovation
outline.gist: Early scholars accepted a praiseworthy innovation; he prefers keeping bid'ah negative and naming helpful new services differently.

outline.heading: The man who vowed to stand in the sun
outline.gist: The Prophet told him to sit, take shade and speak, keeping only the fast, the one valid act of worship in his vow.

outline.heading: The three men who wanted to outdo the Sunnah
outline.gist: Praying all night, fasting forever and never marrying: whoever turns from my way is not of me.

outline.heading: Monasticism they invented
outline.gist: The only Quranic mention of the term: celibacy Allah did not prescribe, which they could not keep and which led to harm.

outline.heading: A working definition
outline.gist: An invented path in the deen claimed equal to Allah's law, meant to exaggerate worship.

outline.heading: Rituals are strict; their form can flex
outline.gist: No new rituals, but doing an existing act such as dua publicly for people's benefit is not bid'ah.

outline.heading: Umar unites the tarawih
outline.gist: Umar gathered scattered worshippers behind one reciter without hesitation; insisting on eight rakat misses the spirit.

outline.heading: Weekly complaints about communal recitation
outline.gist: Setting up a recitation service is not claiming a new act of worship; the rigid view is a movement of the last century.

outline.heading: Public interest and the absence of the Prophet
outline.gist: Maslahah is a source of rulings, and an ummah without the Prophet's presence needs exercises and teaching he did not need.

outline.heading: Creative solutions labelled by scholars
outline.gist: The objectives of religion guide what is acceptable; students should learn before starting initiatives or condemning them.

outline.heading: Telling bid'ah apart from other categories
outline.gist: Distinguish heresy and dysfunctional exaggeration from legitimate differences, self-purification exercises, services and sins.

outline.heading: Good deeds reduced to rituals and aid
outline.gist: Praying, fasting and handing out aid are good deeds, but not the whole of it.

outline.heading: Salih means functional
outline.gist: A lamp that gives no light is not salih; a man praying in the masjid while his brother feeds him was told his brother was better.

outline.heading: Today's function: the state of the ummah
outline.gist: Any act, even worship, not aimed at strengthening the ummah and lifting oppression from Palestine and elsewhere is a waste.

outline.heading: Masajid without people to serve
outline.gist: Building ever more masajid means little without imams, mentors and support for those in need; Ramadan crowds vanish without retention.

outline.heading: Water fountains and empty masajid in Syria
outline.gist: Charity reduced to fountains and buildings that no one fills with work.

outline.heading: Outro

ymw0zaVDVAA.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 29: Ninth Night of Tahajjud
ymw0zaVDVAA.one_line: Why the Prophet and his companions loved long night prayer, and how to stand in prayer as a privilege rather than a chore.
ymw0zaVDVAA.summary: The first reminder starts from narrations of the Prophet's chest sounding like a boiling pot as he held back tears in prayer, and of Abu Bakr being too tender to lead the people without weeping. The companions stood for hours night after night, and the sheikh argues no one can discipline himself into that: they enjoyed it, as the Prophet's call to Bilal to give them rest through prayer shows. He then defines the attitude that makes this possible as agreement, acceptance and acknowledgement. Using the example of being sent out on an errand when already in bed, he shows that the action gets done either way; what differs is whether you do it resentful or grateful. Prayer is a given, so the question is how you stand: as a God-given privilege that could be taken at any moment. It is not about tears but about peace, reaching the point where you are not watching the clock because there is nowhere else you would rather be. In a second reminder he narrates the Prophet's dua for Aisha's forgiveness and his words that this is his dua for his ummah in every prayer. A brief third note tells followers that the imam carries their small slips, so they can give themselves to the prayer.

outline.heading: Interlude
Weeping held back in the Prophet's prayer
outline.gist: Aisha describes a sound from the Prophet's chest like a boiling pot as he fought his emotions to keep reciting audibly, and Abu Bakr was a man too tender to lead the prayer without weeping.

outline.heading: They prayed for hours because they enjoyed it
outline.gist: No one can discipline himself into standing for hours night after night; the Prophet and his companions loved it, as his words to Bilal about finding rest in prayer show.

outline.heading: Agreement, acceptance, acknowledgement: the errand example
outline.gist: Sent out on an urgent errand when already in bed, you will go regardless; whether you go cursing or grateful depends on whether you accept that it needs doing now.

outline.heading: Prayer as a God-given privilege
outline.gist: Praying is a given; the question is the attitude, and it should be seen as a privilege that makes you beyond fortunate, not as a burden or a necessity.

outline.heading: It is not about the tears
outline.gist: Some stop praying at night when tears no longer come, but the aim is to stand in complete peace, grateful for the chance that could be taken away at any moment.

outline.heading: When there is nowhere else you would rather be
outline.gist: Watching the clock and wanting the imam to finish is the opposite state; when absorbed in something you love, as people are in gaming, hours pass unnoticed, and that absorption is what to seek in prayer.

outline.heading: Start from gratitude, not from forcing a feeling
outline.gist: Standing there trying to produce emotion comes at it from the wrong end; begin by asking whether you feel fortunate, grateful and blessed to be standing where you are.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Prophet's dua for Aisha and for his ummah
outline.gist: Seeing him in good spirits, Aisha asked for a dua and he asked forgiveness for all her sins, past and future, hidden and open; she laughed with joy, and he told her this is his dua for his ummah in every prayer.

outline.heading: Interlude
Behind the imam, he carries your slips
outline.gist: Almost nothing invalidates a follower's prayer except deliberately moving ahead of the imam; mistakes such as standing up too early are borne by him, which frees the follower to give himself to the prayer.

outline.heading: Interlude
Outro

themes.label: Spirituality, khushoo and the inner life
themes.note: Long night prayer is sustained by love and inner peace rather than discipline or the pursuit of tears.

themes.label: Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance
themes.note: The prayer is a given; what matters is standing in it with agreement, acceptance and acknowledgement of its worth.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: Being able to stand in prayer is a privilege that could be taken away at any moment, and should be met with thankfulness.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: The right starting point in prayer is feeling fortunate and blessed to be standing there.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: The Prophet wept in prayer and found rest in it, and his companions shared that love of long standing.

themes.label: Dua and invocation
themes.note: The Prophet asked forgiveness for Aisha and for his whole ummah in every prayer.

themes.label: Jurisprudence rulings and how to approach fiqh
themes.note: In congregation the imam bears the follower's slips; only deliberately moving ahead of him harms the prayer.

hadith.gist: When the Prophet prayed, a sound like the boiling of a pot was heard from his chest from weeping.
When the Prophet said to tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer, Aisha said Abu Bakr is a tender man who would weep and not be heard.
Give us rest through it, O Bilal (said of calling the prayer).

Aisha asked the Prophet for a dua; he said: O Allah, forgive Aisha what she has done before and after, in secret and in the open. When she laughed with joy he said this is his dua for his ummah in every prayer.

maxims: Agreement, acceptance and acknowledgement
Doing the action is a given; the question is how
It's really not about the tears
Prayer is a God-given privilege
takeaways: Stand in prayer as someone fortunate to be there, not as someone waiting for it to end.
Do not judge or abandon night prayer by whether tears come; aim for peace and presence.
Begin each prayer from gratitude for being able to stand before Allah instead of trying to force a feeling.
Remember that the Prophet included his ummah in his dua for forgiveness in every prayer.
In congregation, stop worrying over small slips and only take care not to move ahead of the imam.

25:62.ar: وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِي جَعَلَ ٱلَّيۡلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَ خِلۡفَةࣰ لِّمَنۡ أَرَادَ أَن يَذَّكَّرَ أَوۡ أَرَادَ شُكُورࣰ ا
25:62.en: And He it is Who hath appointed night and day in succession, for him who desireth to remember, or desireth thankfulness

25:73.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِّرُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ رَبِّهِمۡ لَمۡ يَخِرُّواْ عَلَيۡهَا صُمࣰّ ا وَعُمۡيَانࣰ ا
25:73.en: And those who, when they are reminded of the revelations of their Lord, fall not deaf and blind thereat

2:254.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ أَنفِقُواْ مِمَّا رَزَقۡنَٰكُم مِّن قَبۡلِ أَن يَأۡتِيَ يَوۡمࣱ لَّا بَيۡعࣱ فِيهِ وَلَا خُلَّةࣱ وَلَا شَفَٰعَةࣱۗ وَٱلۡكَٰفِرُونَ هُمُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
2:254.en: O ye who believe! spend of that wherewith We have provided you ere a day come when there will be no trafficking, nor friendship, nor intercession. The disbelievers, they are the wrong-doers

2:255.ar: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلۡحَيُّ ٱلۡقَيُّومُۚ لَا تَأۡخُذُهُۥ سِنَةࣱ وَلَا نَوۡمࣱۚ لَّهُۥ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۗ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِي يَشۡفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذۡنِهِۦۚ يَعۡلَمُ مَا بَيۡنَ أَيۡدِيهِمۡ وَمَا خَلۡفَهُمۡۖ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيۡءࣲ مِّنۡ عِلۡمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَۚ وَسِعَ كُرۡسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَۖ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفۡظُهُمَاۚ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَلِيُّ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ
2:255.en: Allah! There is no deity save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth. Who is he that intercedeth with Him save by His leave? He knoweth that which is in front of them and that which is behind them, while they encompass nothing of His knowledge save what He will. His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them. He is the Sublime, the Tremendous

2:261.ar: مَّثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمۡوَٰلَهُمۡ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أَنۢبَتَتۡ سَبۡعَ سَنَابِلَ فِي كُلِّ سُنۢبُلَةࣲ مِّاْئَةُ حَبَّةࣲۗ وَٱللَّهُ يُضَٰعِفُ لِمَن يَشَآءُۚ وَٱللَّهُ وَٰسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ
2:261.en: The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. Allah giveth increase manifold to whom He will. Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing

3:92.ar: لَن تَنَالُواْ ٱلۡبِرَّ حَتَّىٰ تُنفِقُواْ مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَۚ وَمَا تُنفِقُواْ مِن شَيۡءࣲ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِهِۦ عَلِيمࣱ‏
3:92.en: Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love. And whatsoever ye spend, Allah is Aware thereof

2:259.ar: أَوۡ كَٱلَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَىٰ قَرۡيَةࣲ وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا قَالَ أَنَّىٰ يُحۡيِۦ هَٰذِهِ ٱللَّهُ بَعۡدَ مَوۡتِهَاۖ فَأَمَاتَهُ ٱللَّهُ مِاْئَةَ عَامࣲ ثُمَّ بَعَثَهُۥۖ قَالَ كَمۡ لَبِثۡتَۖ قَالَ لَبِثۡتُ يَوۡمًا أَوۡ بَعۡضَ يَوۡمࣲۖ قَالَ بَل لَّبِثۡتَ مِاْئَةَ عَامࣲ فَٱنظُرۡ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِكَ وَشَرَابِكَ لَمۡ يَتَسَنَّهۡۖ وَٱنظُرۡ إِلَىٰ حِمَارِكَ وَلِنَجۡعَلَكَ ءَايَةࣰ لِّلنَّاسِۖ وَٱنظُرۡ إِلَى ٱلۡعِظَامِ كَيۡفَ نُنشِزُهَا ثُمَّ نَكۡسُوهَا لَحۡمࣰ اۚ فَلَمَّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُۥ قَالَ أَعۡلَمُ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرࣱ‏
2:259.en: Or (bethink thee of) the like of him who, passing by a township which had fallen into utter ruin, exclaimed: How shall Allah give this township life after its death? And Allah made him die a hundred years, then brought him back to life. He said: How long hast thou tarried? (The man) said: I have tarried a day or part of a day. (He) said: Nay, but thou hast tarried for a hundred years. Just look at thy food and drink which have not rotted! Look at thine ass! And, that We may make thee a token unto mankind, look at the bones, how We adjust them and then cover them with flesh! And when (the matter) became clear unto him, he said: I know now that Allah is Able to do all things

36:82.ar: إِنَّمَآ أَمۡرُهُۥٓ إِذَآ أَرَادَ شَيۡـًٔا أَن يَقُولَ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ
36:82.en: But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is
